front: You have 40 samples and 60 features. Can you use the least-squares closed form? Why?
back: No: the rank of X is at most 40 \(\lt\) 60, so \(X^\top X\) is singular.
explanation: More features than samples always breaks invertibility, regardless of the data.

front: Which condition from ch01 fails when d \(\gt\) n, and how does ch02 restore solvability?
back: Linear independence of the columns (ch01, §1.3); ridge adds \(\lambda I\) so the system is always solvable.
explanation: Correlated features fail the same condition softly: XᵀX is invertible but ill-conditioned.

front: The ridge estimate is {{c1::\((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y\)}}.
explanation: With \(\lambda = 0\) it reduces to ordinary least squares.

front: Why is \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) invertible for every \(\lambda \gt 0\)?
back: Adding \(\lambda I\) raises every eigenvalue of the positive semidefinite \(X^\top X\) by \(\lambda\), so all eigenvalues are positive.
explanation: A matrix with all positive eigenvalues is positive definite, hence invertible (exercise 2.1).

front: Set the gradient of \(\|y - Xw\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2\) to zero. Which linear system do you get?
explanation: The gradient is \(-2X^\top(y - Xw) + 2\lambda w\): the penalty adds \(\lambda w\) to the normal equations.

front: Ridge is fitted on raw features measured in metres and in millimetres. What goes wrong?
back: The penalty treats all weights alike, so a feature's units change how strongly it is shrunk. Standardize first.
explanation: The intercept is also left out of the penalty.

front: Least squares plus a penalty \(\lambda\|w\|_2^2\) is called…?
explanation: Introduced by Hoerl and Kennard (1970) for problems with correlated predictors.

front: Ridge vs lasso: what happens to the weights as \(\lambda\) grows?
back: Ridge shrinks them smoothly toward zero, rarely reaching it; lasso sets more and more of them exactly to zero.
explanation: The deciding difference is the penalty: squared values versus absolute values.

front: You expect only a handful of 200 features to matter and you want an interpretable model. Ridge or lasso?
explanation: Its exact zeros perform feature selection; ridge would keep all 200 weights non-zero.

front: Why does the lasso have no closed-form solution in general, unlike ridge?
back: The absolute value is not differentiable at zero, so setting a gradient to zero does not give a linear system.
explanation: It is solved iteratively, typically by coordinate descent.

front: A student standardizes the whole dataset, then runs 5-fold cross-validation to choose \(\lambda\). What is wrong?
back: The means and standard deviations include the validation folds, so validation information leaks into the model.
explanation: Fit every data-dependent preprocessing step on the training folds only (exercise 2.3).

front: Why does a larger \(\lambda\) increase bias but reduce variance?
back: A stronger penalty makes the estimate less sensitive to which sample you drew, at the cost of pulling it away from the unpenalized optimum.
explanation: This is the bias–variance trade-off that cross-validation navigates.

front: Cross-validation error is lowest at the largest \(\lambda\) in your grid. What do you do?
back: Extend the grid to larger values and search again.
explanation: The optimum may lie outside the range you tried.
